Unfortunately almost every puzzle is not an actual in-depth exploration of the mechanic, but is a series of pass/fail knowledge checks where you are going to fail the puzzles the first time you see them because you lack critical information.

Very good puzzle game. Like everyone, I saw the Portal inspiration.
The vibe was similar but not as creepy. The rooms are very white, which isn’t bad, but it feels a bit too sterile—it lacks personality. That said, I like these white walls because they give a void-like atmosphere.

The levels are well-balanced: not too difficult, not too easy, and always fun. There are a few levels where speed is required, and I didn’t enjoy those as much. The timing felt strict, especially when playing with a controller. I had to switch to mouse and keyboard, where I’m more comfortable with these mechanical challenges.

One flaw I noticed—and I got used to it quickly, so it’s not a huge issue—is that there are softlocks in almost every level. If you make a mistake, you’re forced to restart the level, which happens often.

Overall, it was a very good experience—better than I expected. I recommend it if you liked the Portal franchise or puzzle games in general.

I'm mixed, but erring on positive. I paid just over £2 for this because of a sale, and it was worth it, but it's not a perfect game. Set aside 4 hours and you can 100% it which I think is probably the best way to play it.

The colour mechanics are clever, and intuitive, and they make good use of them. There's a bit too much repetition in the very early levels but after that the puzzles were generally unique enough to be interesting, despite there being very few different pieces for them to work with.

The mechanics unfortunately mean that it's very possible (even easy sometimes) to softlock yourself and have to restart the level. Levels are short, so I didn't find it as bad as some other reviewers, but it is there, and it can be a bit frustrating. What I had more trouble with is how often you need to fire accurately, in the right colour, while under pressure. I did ragequit a few times because of that, but came back a few minutes later.

Another issue is I completed a couple of levels the wrong way by accident, basically skipping the puzzle. Those could have done with a bit more playtesting and tweaking I think.

It looks nice enough, and it works well with a 2560x1080 resolution, which isn't always a given. The voice acting is pretty good. I don't think I ever laughed, but it helps.

Overall it's a decent puzzle game. It's not one of my favourites - there's workshop support with user-made levels, but I'm not interested in playing more. But it's worth a try if you like this sort of thing and want a game you can complete in a short time. (And you'll enjoy it more if you're not so clumsy and panicky as me!) There's a sequel announced which looks a lot more elaborate so I hope they manage to make that a success.

I'm giving this game a "not recommended" only because I, personally, [b]generally[/b] wouldn't recommend it, although I believe there are people out there who would enjoy this game.

I cannot stress this enough: I do not consider this game to be [b]bad[/b]. For what the developers clearly were intending to build, they nailed it: Its mechanics are (mostly) well-established, and it isn't glitchy.  But there are enough problems that I don't really consider it to be good, either.

[h1]Similarities to Portal[/h1]

This is yet another game that was obviously [b]heavily[/b] inspired by Portal, practically to the point of being a knock-off:

[list]
[*]A narrator with the ethics and morals of either GlaDOS or Cave Johnson.
[*]All puzzles are in the vein of "testing".
[*]A magic sci-fi gun that you use to manipulate the environment in order to solve the puzzles/complete the tests
[*]Lethal environmental hazards and puzzle elements (with no real explanation.  At least Aperture had an excuse.)
[*][spoiler]Halfway through the game, the facility undergoes a self-destruct and you have to run for your life to progress[/spoiler]
[/list]

[h1]Game Mechanics[/h1]

[h2]The Gun[/h2]

You've got a sci-fi gun that shoots, er, colors.  Just like Portal, where you start off with a limited gun, you initially can only shoot one color (I think it was red.)  Later on, you get the full Red, Green, and Yellow.

[ul]
[li]Colors mix [b]subtractively[/b], like paint: White + (any color) = That color.  Any color + itself = that color.  Red + Yellow = Orange, Red + Blue = Purple, Blue + Yellow = Green.  Any other combo makes what the game calls "brown" but is really a very dark grey, like ash.  (This includes things like Green + Blue or Purple + Red, depsite the fact that this makes no sense.)
[li]You can paint any wall, floor bump, or "living" worker droid (more on this later) with any color your gun possesses, unless that wall or droid has a hexagonal "shield" around it.
[/ul]

[h2]Doors & Door triggers[/h2]

Some doors open automatically when you approach, but like Portal, most of them are connected to one or more triggers, in which case [b]all[/b] connected triggers must be active in order to open the door.

There are two ways to activate a trigger: first, you can step on it, and second, you can get a worker droid to hover over it.

The first is rarely useful; unless a trigger is directly in front of the door it opens, as soon as you step off, the door closes again.  (This comes into play sometimes in later puzzles.)  As such, you will mostly be using worker droids for these.

[h2]Worker Droids[/h2]

Worker droids are floating spheres.  Despite their name, they do no actual work.  There is no narrative explanation for their existence, apart from their use in completing the "tests".  About 95% of the game is manipulating these things into position.

Worker droids are attracted to nearby walls that are the same color as the droid, [b]unless[/b] that color is the dark gray resulting from an bad color mix.  When there are multiple nearby walls, they pull on the droid equally, allowing you to manipulate them into entering the center of the
room.

Worker droids come in two flavors: harmless and vicious.

Harmless droids are ordinary spheres and will only move when the color-matching rules dictate that they are to do so.

Vicious droids are spheres with spikes around them.  Hitting them with paint, or forcing them to move by painting a nearby wall, will make them angry.   Angry droids will chase after you and melee you to death, unless they are pulled to a wall by the color-matching rules.  Narratively, their existence is explained away with "whoops, we made a mistake, oh well."

[h2]Electrified Floor Plates[/h2]

Some puzzles feature electrified floor plates.  They are [b]one-shot[/b] instakill for whatever passes over them, after which they become harmless. (PROTIP: Make sure that's not you.)  There is no narrative explanation given whatsoever for their existence.  Sometimes you need to manipulate droids to pass over them, destroying the droid and neutralizing the plate.  Sometimes they serve as an obstacle and you need to control your painting so droids don't run into them. 

[h2]Transparent Barriers[/h2]

These are never explained at all, but there are transparent barriers that you and the droids cannot pass through, but you can shoot paint through them.

[h2]Transparent Glass[/h2]
This is always associated with a foot-high wall on the floor. You can see through it, but you can't shoot through it.

[h2]Color-reset devices[/h2]

These show up without any narrative introduction or explanation.  About halfway through the game, you will see devices on some walls -- they actually look like the cameras from Portal -- that, if the wall they are attached to is (re)painted, they wake up and restore the wall to its original color.  (For nearly all of them, the original color is white, but there are a few exceptions.)  

This is different from the hexagonal "no-paint" barrier because the device takes about 5 seconds to wake up.

[h2]Reflectors[/h2]

These show up in the last chapter, and are only used twice, which is good, because I [b]hate[/b] them.

Like the color-reset devices, they are given no introduction or explanation.  They look kind of like targets hanging on a wall; if you shoot a wall that has a reflector on it, the wall will be painted as usual, but also, the paint will rebound from the wall to another wall.  They're extremely difficult to use properly, mostly because you can't actually see where the rebound will land, which means trial-and-error.

[h1]The Problems[/h1]

I encountered a number of problems with the game itself.

[h2]It's boring[/h2]

The entire game, from beginning to end, is one long "testing track".  Even in the middle of the game, [spoiler]when the facility is suddenly self-destructing (which stops and then things go back to normal with no explanation whatsoever)[/spoiler].

There is very little variety to these rooms; they all have a general [i]sameness[/i] to them.  The game is divided up into 8 "chapters" which seem to be completely arbitrary in their delination.

One of the last few puzzles requires that you go through five different doors.  These doors are opened by a "clock" constructed nearby created from a group of worker droids that, under their color-movement rules, proceed endlessly through a large circle.  It's a really cool concept and you can only see a tiny little part of it and you have to sit there waiting [b]ages[/b] for the doors to open up so you can go through and solve the sub-puzzles within.  And once you've solved each sub-puzzle, you can't leave again until the droid clock reopens the door.   I spent quite a bit of time in this level simply waiting.

[h2]It's very unforgiving of mistakes[/h2]

In Portal, if you place a portal on the wrong wall, or with the wrong orientation, you can just fire again to fix it.

However, except for walls where there's a color-reset device, the change made by painting a wall or droid is permanent.  The nature of the paint rules means that in many cases, the slightest mistake (wrong color, wrong wall, wrong droid, but mostly wrong color) means you have to restart the entire puzzle.

In fact...

[h2]Failure is Mandatory[/h2]

There were several puzzles that I'm quite certain cannot be reliably solved from the beginning without prior knowledge from earlier attempts.  The worst of them were...

[h2]Time for disaster[/h2]

...[b]timed puzzles[/b].  There a quite a few puzzles where you are racing against a clock.   In two cases, you are racing against an explicit clock, but there are also several cases that stand out where the clock is implicit between the color reset devices and the movement speed of the droids.

I never cleared any of these the first try: I had to fail to learn enough information to know how to solve them.

ChromaGun can best be described as "meh". As a lover of first person puzzle games, I went into this with moderately high expectations, and while ChromaGun isn't the worst game ever, it is overall very mediocre. I played on Steam Deck, and had no issues getting the game to run.

The gameplay premise is simple - armed with a color gun that can shoot blue, yellow, and red, you are supposed to solve puzzles by directing colored drones to switches in every room. Shoot a wall red, and a red drone will move towards it - shoot multiple walls red and the drone will go to the middle point between the walls. It is a simple premise that is very interesting at first.

There are a few problems with the puzzles though. First, they are altogether way too easy. Only a few rooms can be problematic, and that's because you are either under a timer or because there is some tight maneuvering with the drones needed. The second problem, and that exacerbates most issues I have with the game, is that there is a lack of QOL features. If you make a mistake in the room, you can't erase a color or undo things - you have to restart the entire level. With some levels relying on timing or locking you in rooms because of timed walls or switches, this means that a single mistake means you have to repeat everything you have done before. 

It is baffling to me that this gun has no way to remove paint from a wall - this alone would have made many of the puzzles so much smoother; the ability to undo mistakes that every other puzzle game has is simply missing. There is also a frustrating idle pose - if you stand still for just a few seconds, like for analyzing a puzzle, the protagonist raises the gun for an inspection, which blocks half the screen for a few seconds. Why?

Since you can't erase colors, many of the puzzle solutions rely on you to simply continue mixing colors into a wall, for example to detach a drone from it. It feels weird to mix all three colors together into black to detach an orange drone from a wall, instead of just being able to erase the color. It feels often unintentional despite being completely intentional.

So the puzzling is mediocre, but sadly, so is the story. The game is clearly trying to do a Portal thing, with a voice guiding you from puzzle to puzzle, with some really cringy dialogue that tries way too hard to do the "quirky corporation that just wants lab rats" thing. Funny enough, you actually do risk your life several times during the game, only for the end to be 
[spoiler] the guy essentially offering you a job. What makes you think I want that after almost dying several times, without you really helping me at all? [/spoiler].

We don't really know what this corporation does, we don't know why we are a test subject, we don't know why we are risking our life. The story is paper thin and never captures you, unlike in Portal or even games like The Entropy Centre. You just solve room after room, without ever really knowing why.

So in short, ChromaGun is a very easy game with a few frustrating puzzle outliers, a paper thin story and some sorely missing QOL (if you can describe being able to undo mistakes as QOL, I feel like that is essential). It is also very short and can be finished in 2-3 hours. Overall, I would give this a pass and play some of the many better first person puzzle games - this one needs to be a lot more fleshed out to be fun and engaging.
